new_statements.translation: Accent. Prosodic accent is a strong phonological mark in Spanish [...]. We therefore assume that the accent that Guanche toponyms keep today, as we know them from oral tradition, is more faithful to the Guanche original than the vowels and consonants that make them up. [...] Equally striking is the long series of words with antepenultimate (esdrújula) stress preserved in El Hierro, a prosody so foreign to the morphology of common, popular Spanish [...]. If in El Hierro it is the antepenult-stressed words that stand out, in La Gomera it is the toponyms that end in a stressed vowel, mostly in -é but also in -á.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional rule is stated or recoverable. Guanche is extinct and known only through Hispanicised toponyms, anthroponyms and a few phrases; the authors hold that the stress of surviving oral toponyms is probably original, and that alongside the (Spanish-like, unremarked) penultimate majority there are island-specific clusters of antepenultimate stress (El Hierro: Arétique, Bérote, Itámote, Tembárgena; colour terms cómbaca, ómana, mástuca) and final stress (La Gomera: Aradá, Chejeré, Chelé; fewer in Tenerife: Fañabé, Guiné), plus many doublets differing only in stress (Atosar/Atósar, Beñamo/Béñamo). Ballester 2003 (pp. 12-14) independently reconstructs many proparoxytones and 'muchas más formas no oxítonas' ending in -d/-n/-r than Castilian allows (Güímar, tagóror, Jinámar); Acosta Armas 2017 (p. 23 n. 24) states the tonic syllable of a guanchismo can hardly be known because the chronicles do not mark accent. Net: stress position lexically variable in the surviving corpus and not reducible to a rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Doublets with accent shift (Áfite/Afite, Ajifio/Ajifío, Anjúa/Anjua, Atosar/Atósar, Bedio/Bedío, Beñamo/Béñamo, Birama/Bírama, Brasía/Brasia, Eris/Erís, Güime/Goíme, Gusano/Gúsano); §15 warns that written/cartographic forms carry many accent errors (Jinámar GC vs Jinama EH; Julan not Julán; Marsagán, Tesén, Arguineguín, Mogán). Ballester adds the caveat that unmarked accent in old Castilian spelling may have produced spelling-pronunciations.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the word accent of Guanche-origin toponyms and appellatives as pronounced today in Canarian Spanish oral tradition (citation forms), used as a proxy for the extinct language; not phrase-level. Island differences (El Hierro antepenult, La Gomera/Tenerife final) may reflect inter-island dialect differences of the pre-Hispanic language(s).
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern the pre-Hispanic language(s) of the Canary Islands (Glottolog guan1277 'Guanche', iso gnc, used in the broad sense for all seven islands, not only Tenerife) as reflected in Guanche-origin toponyms and appellatives surviving in present-day Canarian Spanish; the accent observations are island-specific (antepenultimate cluster in El Hierro, final-stress cluster in La Gomera and to a lesser degree Tenerife), which the authors treat as possibly reflecting inter-island dialect differences. No living speakers; evidence is 15th-17th c. chronicle spellings (mostly without accent marks; Espinosa 1594 marks some) plus modern oral toponymy.
